A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InftyThink framework and data-reconstruction pipeline. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and matchable despite reorganization and revised experimental settings.

before.justification: v3 reports original fine-tuning experiments across five models, benchmark results in Table 1, and segmentation, RoPE, and computational-cost analyses.

after.justification: v4 reports original benchmark experiments, summarizer and data-quantity controls, repeated-training results, and additional mathematical and coding evaluations.

M1.justification: The segmentation, summary generation, training-instance construction, and inference using the preceding summary remain substantively unchanged. Renamed dialogue tags and max_epochs/max_iters do not introduce a new procedure; changed iteration limits are experimental budgets.

E1.justification: v4 adds OpenThoughts training experiments and evaluations on AIME25, Math Odyssey, and AMC23. Appendix L extends coverage beyond mathematical and scientific reasoning to HumanEval and MBPP coding tasks, including their Plus tests.

E2.justification: Vanilla reasoning and RoPE interpolation are retained. v4 adds unmodified instruction-tuned checkpoints in Table 1 and numerical comparisons with Merging-0.6, Thinkless, HBPO, AdaR1, AdaptThink, and TLMRE in Table 11. The latter use cross-study reported results, with acknowledged evaluation differences and no common-environment timing comparison.

E3.justification: v3 Appendix B versus v4 Appendix M changes vanilla's output cap from 16,384 to 32,768 tokens and InftyThink's iteration cap from 50 to 10. LAT replaces TPS, measuring total evaluation wall time per sampled generation. New studies also introduce EOS-based context-hit measurement, resampling controls, alternative summarizers, and instruction-tuned starting checkpoints.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained segmentation, RoPE, iteration, and computational-cost analyses, v4 adds context-truncation analysis, summarizer-size ablations, and training-data oversampling/downsampling controls in Appendices D–G. Appendix J adds iteration trajectories on three further mathematical benchmarks.

E5.justification: Both versions report 16 evaluation samples per instance at temperature 0.7. v4 additionally reports three training runs with individual accuracies in Table 6 and discusses training variability. This limited stability study does not establish repeated training for every main-table configuration; confidence intervals and significance tests remain absent.

E6.justification: Under revised inference caps, Table 1's Qwen2.5-Math-7B AIME24 vanilla/InftyThink accuracies change from 26.46/40.00 to 32.92/43.96. Table 2's best AIME24 segmentation changes from 2k to 4k. The retained RoPE score of 30.63 now falls below vanilla's 32.92. v4 also adds substantial control, stability, benchmark, and comparison results in Tables 3–9 and 11.

T1.justification: v4 introduces an EOS-based definition of context-hit rate in Appendix D and defines LAT as (t2−t1)/(m×n) in Appendix R. These are limited metric-definition additions. The reconstruction equations and token-count/squared-token identities are retained, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The introduction narrows the claimed Qwen2.5-Math-7B gains from approximately 3/13/10 to 2/11/9 percentage points across the three benchmarks; the abstract changes its range from 3–13% to 3–11%. The central contributions and claims about iterative reasoning, bounded context, and computational efficiency remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v4 adds arguments attributing gains to the reasoning paradigm rather than summarizer knowledge or additional training examples, and discusses transfer across training corpora and coding tasks. Appendix Q acknowledges cross-study metric differences and unavailable timing comparisons. The specific claim that smaller segments help AIME24 is removed; the original summarization-loss, coherence, and latency limitations are retained in Appendix A.

D1.justification: v4 supplements the existing implementation information with a dataset access link, top_p=0.95, training-step counts of 6,543 versus 6,257, summarizer construction costs, and chat-template adaptation guidance. The core training framework, optimizer settings, packing procedure, hardware, and summary-generation prompt are retained.

R1.justification: v4 substantially expands the earlier reasoning/compression review with an iterative-methods subsection covering RecurrentGPT, Tree-of-Thoughts, ReAct, and least-to-most prompting. It also adds positioning against reinforcement-learning methods for length control. These are substantive additions beyond the numerous bibliographic publication updates.

P1.justification: Most existing main-text prose and contribution statements are retained. v4 edits terminology and method explanations, changes citation style, moves Discussion from Section 5 to Appendix A, and rearranges the older appendices. The extensive new experiments do not correspond to an extensive rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v4 redesigns Table 1 with base/instruct groups, average columns, and latency reporting; redraws Figure 1's efficiency panel around latency; and adds eight tables and an iteration figure. The document template and table-caption placement change, while existing prompt, distribution, and computational-cost figures are retained with resizing, relocation, and renumbering.

improvement.justification: The summarizer and data-quantity controls in v4 Tables 4–5 address confounds left untested in v3, while coding evaluations and construction-cost disclosures strengthen applicability and reproducibility. Reporting problems temper these benefits: Table 11 labels the 88.06/29.38 results as 1.5B although Table 1 assigns them to 7B, and the broad improvement discussion does not adequately address regressions in revised tables. The controlled evidence supports a limited net improvement.
